inserts.title: Corridor width measures how consistent a route is
paragraphs: A **corridor** is the band of ground a bird covers repeatedly when it flies home along the same learned path. Its width describes how tightly a bird's training tracks cluster around one route. A narrow corridor means the bird returns to nearly the same ground on each journey, whereas a wide corridor means its paths vary more from flight to flight.

Biro and colleagues measured corridor widths from each bird's final training tracks, expressed relative to its route length. The average width was 151 m at Weston Wood and 176 m at High Cogges. Because the width is scaled to the route, routes of different lengths can be compared on one scale.

The corridor width therefore captures consistency in the flight path, not the accuracy of arrival at the loft. A pigeon can stay within a narrow corridor and still take an indirect route, so the width summarizes how repeatable the path is. The GPS records supply this measure directly from the tracks.

inserts.title: Convergence reveals a pull toward a learned corridor
paragraphs: **Convergence** is the movement of a displaced bird back toward a route it has flown before. In an off-route release, the bird begins far from its usual corridor, so any turn toward the old track shows what draws it. Biro and colleagues recorded the complete homing track of each pigeon to see whether it headed straight for the loft or first rejoined the familiar route.

Many off-route tracks merged with the previously used corridor before continuing toward home. The published maps show the training tracks alongside the test tracks at a scale of about 2 km, so each displacement can be read against the surrounding terrain. The merge happened far from the release point, which indicates that the route exerts its pull over a broad area.

The merging supports attraction toward familiar visual landmarks more than a fresh calculation of the shortest course. The pigeon reaches features it recognizes first and follows the route toward the loft afterward. Other navigational systems remained available during the same flights, so the convergence reflects a combination of guidance rather than one signal.

inserts.title: Time-compensated sun compass uses the sun and clock
paragraphs: A **time-compensated sun compass** combines the sun's position with the bird's internal sense of time to estimate a direction. The sun moves across the sky at a steady rate, so the same solar position corresponds to a different compass direction at a different hour. Keeping the internal clock matched to local time keeps the sun compass accurate.

Biro and colleagues shifted the birds' clock by delaying artificial sunrise and sunset by 4 h for 5–7 days. The shift predicted a solar-compass error of about 90° on the release dates. The tracks after treatment were compared with each bird's earlier flights, so every pigeon's own route served as the baseline.

The clock shift sets the sun compass against the landmarks that the bird recognizes. A bird that follows its familiar route ignores part of the compass error, whereas a bird that trusts the compass moves away from the route. The contrast shows that the sun is one source among several that the pigeon combines.

inserts.title: Parallel offsets keep shape while shifting position
paragraphs: A **parallel offset** is a flight that keeps the shape of an earlier route while sitting consistently to one side of it. The bird does not abandon its route for a new straight line. It maintains the sequence of turns and the overall form, and only the position changes.

After the clock shift, some highly familiar pigeons flew parallel to their former tracks on the anticlockwise side. Route-relative vectors measured the lateral offset in metres, with reference rings at 100, 300 and 500 m that make each displacement easy to compare. The offsets were consistent across the birds that showed them.

Parallel offsets indicate that landmark attraction and compass influence act together during the journey. The bird keeps its learned route shape while the compass shifts the whole route sideways. A flight of this kind combines recognition of features with a directional correction.

inserts.title: Olfactory map versus activation hypothesis
paragraphs: An **olfactory map** uses learned odor information to estimate position relative to home, so the smell of a place carries location. An **olfactory activation hypothesis** proposes that the mere experience of unfamiliar odors helps navigation, even when the odors carry no location information. The two accounts predict different results when the odor history is changed.

Gagliardo and colleagues transported pigeons in containers supplied with natural air, charcoal-filtered air or filtered air with artificial plant odors. Artificial odor puffs were supplied about every 20 min during transport and while the birds waited at the release site. Each group therefore carried a different odor history into the release.

The activation account predicts that artificial odors should help as much as natural air. The map account predicts that only the natural mixture helps, because only natural air carries the geographical odor signature. The later tracks decide between these predictions.

inserts.title: Nasal anesthesia applies the same block to all groups
paragraphs: A **nasal block** removes the sense of smell for a short time by anesthetizing the olfactory mucosa. Gagliardo and colleagues applied Xylocaine immediately before release, so every pigeon lost new odor input during early flight. Because the block was the same across groups, any difference between the groups must come from the odors they experienced before release.

The birds had already been exposed to natural air, filtered air or artificial odors during transport and before takeoff. Releases occurred at sites 53 km and 61 km from home. The shared block limited new odor sampling while the earlier exposure differences stayed in place.

This design isolates the effect of prior odor history on navigation. The anesthesia wears off, so the later part of the flight reflects smell returning, and the timing of that recovery is part of the measured flight. The comparison therefore keeps the nasal block constant while the earlier odor history changes.

inserts.title: Bearings and tracks describe different flight phases
paragraphs: A **bearing** is the compass direction in which a released bird disappears from view. It records the first moments of the flight. A complete GPS track instead records the whole journey, including circling, stops, course correction and progress toward home.

Gagliardo and colleagues found that bearings from the early part of each track did not reflect all the differences that appeared over the first hour. At the 53 km release, artificial-odor birds could leave in a set direction and then make little homeward progress. The full track revealed a deficit that the departure alone did not show.

The two measures therefore describe different stages of the same flight. A bird can leave in a reasonable direction and correct later, or leave poorly and recover, so the full track is needed to judge how well it navigated. Each measure is kept separate in the analysis so that the early and late parts of the flight are not confused.

inserts.title: c-Fos maps regional activity, not single neurons
paragraphs: **c-Fos** is an activity-related protein whose presence marks cells that recently fired. Antibody labeling reveals the labeled nuclei, and their density in a region shows how strongly that region was engaged over the hours before sampling. The measure summarizes activity across a region instead of recording the spikes of single cells.

Jorge and colleagues sampled brains 1–2 h after each odor treatment and counted labeled nuclei per square millimetre in the hippocampal formation, olfactory bulb and piriform cortex. Each condition was compared against controls processed the same way. The counts show which regions responded to each treatment.

A regional count shows where activity accumulated across the sampled tissue. The dorsolateral hippocampal area stands out because its labeling tracked the odor treatments most closely, which tells the reader where the response was strongest.

inserts.title: Magnetic stimulation labels trigeminal nuclei
paragraphs: The **trigeminal nerve** carries sensory information from the head to brainstem nuclei. Its ophthalmic branch, V1, sends fibers to the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei. Lefeldt and colleagues used ZENK labeling to ask whether changing magnetic fields activated these nuclei in pigeons.

Pigeons were exposed for 3 h to a constantly changing magnetic field, to a compensated zero field, or to the changing field after bilateral V1 section. ZENK was detected in the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei after each exposure. The pattern of labeling across the three groups shows where the changing field had its effect.

Labeling rose when the field changed and V1 was intact, and it fell when the field was removed or the nerve was cut. The result links the magnetic stimulus to the peripheral sensory pathway that runs through V1. The labeling pattern therefore identifies which nuclei the changing field reached.

inserts.title: Tracing shows a route from V1 to labeled nuclei
paragraphs: **Neuronal tracing** follows the anatomical pathways that leave an injection site. Lefeldt and colleagues injected cholera toxin B into V1 to label its central projections. The labeled fibers were then compared with the regions that showed ZENK after magnetic stimulation.

V1 fibers terminated in the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei, which are the same nuclei that contained ZENK-positive cells. The overlays keep the position of each traced fiber relative to the activation, with scales of 100 µm and 200 µm. Acetylcholinesterase staining marked the nuclear boundaries, so the subdivisions could be located precisely.

The overlap places the magnetic response along a known route from the nerve to the brainstem. Acetylcholinesterase acts here as a marker of boundaries, which keeps the labeled tissue tied to the known anatomy. The labeled fibers and the activated nuclei are compared in the same sections, which keeps the spatial relation intact.

inserts.title: Stains locate iron, not the cell that holds it
paragraphs: **Prussian blue** is a stain that reveals ferric iron in tissue. A stained spot shows where iron accumulates, and a second line of evidence is needed to name the cell that holds it, since iron also appears in metabolic storage and immune cells.

Treiber and colleagues stained pigeon upper beaks with Prussian blue and mapped the labeled cells through serial sections. The stained cells lay in respiratory epithelium, subepidermal tissue and feather follicles. The position of each labeled cell is therefore recorded alongside its tissue.

The stained positions give a map of where iron occurs, which is the first step toward identifying a magnetic receptor. Further markers and ultrastructure then decide whether the stained cells are sensory or storage cells. Each stained location is then examined for the cell type that carries it.

inserts.title: Immune markers test cell identity in beak tissue
paragraphs: **Macrophages** are immune cells that engulf material and take part in tissue defense. MHC II is a cell-surface marker of antigen presentation that several immune cell types express. Treiber and colleagues combined this marker with iron staining to check whether the beak cells were immune cells.

MHC II labeling colocalized with the iron-positive cells in respiratory epithelium, subepidermal tissue and feather follicles. The ultrastructure and the lack of convincing neuronal-marker labeling supported macrophages over magnetosensitive neurons. The micrographs carry a 10 µm scale bar.

Cell identity determines whether iron in a cell can carry magnetic information. An iron-laden macrophage is a storage cell, and that identity rests on several markers taken together across the tissues. Together, the markers and the ultrastructure give a consistent identity for the cells, and the immune identity is what the pigeon-beak data show.

inserts.title: Local field potentials sum population activity
paragraphs: A **local field potential** is an extracellular voltage that reflects coordinated activity in a population of neurons around the electrode. It differs from the spike of one identified neuron, because it sums the currents of many cells at once.

Yang and colleagues recorded hippocampal LFPs and the bird's position at the same time during outdoor homing flights. The electrodes sampled the left hippocampal formation, and the release sites lay more than 0.8 km from the loft. Trials were run in clear weather with low wind.

Recording the population signal during flight allows the neural state to be read against the bird's position and heading. The shared time base is what links a population rhythm to a particular stage of the trip. The population signal therefore reflects the activity of many cells recorded at one electrode.

inserts.title: Band power changes between navigation stages
paragraphs: **Spectral power** measures how much of a recorded voltage falls within a chosen frequency range. Yang and colleagues assigned theta to 4–12 Hz, beta to 12–30 Hz, low gamma to 30–60 Hz and high gamma to 60–120 Hz, so each band has a fixed range.

Theta and beta power ratios were higher in the initial decision-making stage than during en route flight. The high-gamma ratio rose en route, while low gamma showed no consistent difference between stages. The comparisons used paired stages from the same homing flights.

The stages therefore differ in how power is distributed across the bands, rather than in a single overall increase. Each band reflects a separate pattern of population activity, and the stage contrast depends on the band selected.

2: **Homing** is navigation back to a familiar home after displacement. In pigeons, a **map** estimates position relative to home, whereas a **compass** supplies a directional reference. Each term names a function rather than a physical structure, so a map can work without a complete mental picture of the landscape. A bird can use both systems together, and the two answer different questions about the same journey.

Biro and colleagues recorded homing pigeons with a global positioning system, or GPS, logging position every 1 s. Repeated releases and off-route tests separated the following of a familiar corridor from taking the shortest available course home. The tracks therefore show how a bird moves through a landscape it knows, not only where it ends up.

Birds repeatedly used individually distinctive routes rather than converging on one direct line. Route guidance of this kind can coexist with other sources of location and compass information. The GPS tracks describe the route itself, while the first sensory signal used at an unfamiliar release site is measured by separate tests.
3: **Route fidelity** is the repeated use of a similar path by the same animal. It is distinct from accuracy of arrival, because a pigeon can reach home along a reliable but indirect corridor. Biro and colleagues compared the last three training flights from each release site, which allowed the stability of each bird's path to be measured across many journeys.

After repeated homing experience, mean corridor widths were 151 m at Weston Wood and 176 m at High Cogges. These widths describe the area enclosed by each bird's final training tracks relative to its route length. The narrow widths show how consistently a pigeon returns to the same band of ground.

Tracks from the same bird were more similar to each other than tracks from different birds. Individuality points away from a single obligatory physical corridor. Shared terrain and weather constrain the available paths, yet each pigeon settles on its own route through them.
4: **Route efficiency** compares the direct home distance with the distance actually flown. A lower value means a longer journey, even when the bird reaches the loft. Efficiency and fidelity therefore measure different properties of successful homing, so a bird can be consistent and still indirect.

Biro and colleagues found that final training routes remained indirect after 20 successive releases. Birds flew about 18–25% farther than the direct home distance while continuing to reproduce their individually distinctive paths. The GPS records kept the turns that a single departure bearing would miss.

Persistent detours support **learned route guidance** rather than a gradual convergence on the shortest path. The detours show that a learned corridor can outweigh the straight-line option. The ecological cost of the longer flights depends on factors such as visual reliability and risk along each route, and the study's measurements focus on the flight paths themselves.
5: A displacement away from a trained release point separates recognition of the starting location from recognition of features along an established route. Biro and colleagues released trained pigeons at positions outside their preferred corridors and recorded the complete homing tracks. Each track shows whether the bird heads for the loft directly or first returns to familiar ground.

The off-route tracks often converged on the previously used route before continuing toward the loft. The maps include both the training tracks and the later test tracks, which allows each displacement to be compared with the surrounding landscape. The convergence occurred over a scale of about 2 km, so the pull of the route acts across a wide area.

Convergence fits attraction toward familiar visual landmarks rather than a newly selected direct course from the test site. Every off-route flight also drew on other navigational systems, which stayed available throughout the journey and helped each bird reach the loft.
6: **Visual pilotage** means using recognized landscape features to guide movement along a familiar route. A landmark can provide local guidance without placing the bird in a universal coordinate system. The route is learned as a succession of familiar places, and each place cues the next leg of the journey.

Biro and colleagues compared repeated training flights with off-route releases in the same landscape. Birds were drawn toward their preferred corridors even when that meant an indirect journey. The deviations were large compared with the small fluctuations around a single straight course, which shows that the corridors govern the flight.

The behavior supports route-based visual guidance, and the GPS tracks show how each bird moves along it. Each turn of the route is linked to a feature that the bird has learned. The sequence of those features forms the route memory that drives the flight.
7: A common landscape can constrain flight without forcing all birds onto identical routes. Comparing different pigeons within the same terrain separates a shared environmental influence from an individual's accumulated experience with particular features. The shared terrain sets the outer bounds, and the learned route sets the path inside them.

The training and off-route maps contain clearly different paths for pigeons returning to the same loft. Within-bird training corridors averaged 151 m at Weston Wood, whereas routes from different birds overlapped much less. The geographical target was shared, while each bird's preferred trajectory was its own.

This comparison supports an acquired route memory rather than a single obligatory terrain channel. The individual corridors show that experience shapes each pigeon's path, and the same destination can be reached along many different learned routes.
8: A time-compensated sun compass uses the sun's position together with internal time to estimate direction. Because the solar position changes across the day, altering the bird's internal clock changes the direction it infers while the landscape stays the same. The clock therefore becomes a source of directional conflict.

Biro and colleagues delayed artificial sunrise and sunset by 4 h for 5–7 days. This treatment predicted a solar-compass error of approximately 90° on the release dates. GPS tracks after treatment were compared with each bird's own earlier flights, so every pigeon served as its own control.

The manipulation sets a familiar visual route against the compass information. A displaced course shows that the bird keeps using time-dependent directional information even when it conflicts with the landmarks it knows. The landmarks and other cues remain present, so the sun is one of several sources the bird combines.
9: **Cue weighting** describes the relative influence of different information sources on behavior. It can operate without a conscious decision or a single neuron that assigns numerical weights. Familiarity can change how strongly a recognized route constrains compass-guided movement, which makes the balance between cues depend on experience.

Biro and colleagues compared high-familiarity birds with low-familiarity birds at four sites 5.1–10.6 km from the loft. After the same clock shift, highly familiar birds generally stayed closer to their previous tracks, whereas less familiar birds deviated farther. The contrast shows that experience changes the outcome of the same conflict.

The comparison supports an experience-dependent interaction between landmark guidance and the solar compass. The size of the treatment effect depended on the release site and the layout of the surrounding landscape, so the balance of cues is shaped by both experience and place.
10: A **nearest-neighbour vector** connects a recorded point on one flight to the closest point on a comparison flight. Its length measures the spatial separation between the two flights. Its angle relative to the current flight direction shows whether the bird is displaced to one side or lies ahead or behind its earlier position.

Biro and colleagues calculated these vectors for clock-shifted flights and for earlier GPS tracks.
